newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia court approves new TV law.
newsitem.headline: Colombia court approves new TV law.

text.p: Colombia's constitutional court has upheld a new law to shake-up television programming but eliminated a clause that critics said was tantamount to censorship of news shows.

The court ruled late on Tuesday that programme-makers would not have their contracts automatically renewed and would have to submit fresh bids for broadcast slots on the country's two government-controlled channels.
That will effectively mean all programming, from popular soap operas to TV news, is subject to change beginning on Jan. 1 1998.

All private broadcasters will have to submit bids for new six-year contracts in December to the National Television Commission (CNTV), which critics say is chiefly made up of President Ernesto Samper's supporters.
The biggest bone of contention is the effect the new law could have on morning, evening and weekend news shows -- changing their slots from midweek to weekend or taking them off the air altogther.

In a 5-4 ruling, the Constitutional Court rejected a clause in the law that would have allowed the television commission to carry out a six-monthly review of the "objectivity" of television news shows.

As the law passed through Congress late last year, news directors said the "objectivity" clause would effectively allow the government to gag those news programmes that heavily criticised Samper during the investigation into allegations that he financed his 1994 election campaign with drug money.

Colombian author Gabriel Garcia Marquez, who won the Nobel prize for literature, dubbed it "the most brutal form of censorship on freedom of thought." He is also a shareholder in one of the most overtly anti-Samper TV news shows, QAP.
But in comments to local media on Wednesday, news directors said they still faced the threat of censorship since the television commission could simply refuse them a new contract.

"The decision by the Constitutional Court...means the total triumph of Samper's government," QAP director Maria Isabel Rueda told El Tiempo newspaper. Enrique Santos, one of the heads of El Tiempo and vociferous critic of the new TV law, is also a major shareholder in QAP.
The new TV law, as approved by the constitutional court will also allow for the creation of two private national TV channels and a number of private regional channels.
